item.title: Strategic Brief — August 28, 2026: Glacial Collapse Floods Kill Over 390 on Nepal-Tibet Border as Iran War Hits Six Months With No Off-Ramp
item.description:
Glacial Collapse Floods Kill Over 390 on Nepal-Tibet Border as Iran War Hits Six Months With No Off-Ramp
A Himalayan glacier collapse unleashed catastrophic floods that killed more than 390 people and left over 1,400 missing across the Nepal-China border, while the US-Iran war reached its six-month mark with diplomacy intensifying but no end in sight.
Himalayan Glacier Collapse Kills Over 390, Leaves 1,400 Missing
Catastrophic flash floods triggered by a glacial collapse swept through communities along the Nepal-China border on Wednesday, killing more than 390 people and leaving over 1,400 missing, according to police and rescue officials cited by the Associated Press. The US Geological Survey said the flooding was triggered by a glacial collapse, and scientists' preliminary investigations point to rapidly melting Himalayan ice as the cause, the BBC reports. CCTV footage showed a wall of water and mud several stories high sweeping through Gyirong Port near the border. The disaster has an unusually international dimension: people from more than 30 countries are among the missing, AP reports, and South Korea has dispatched a rapid response team to Nepal as its citizens remain unaccounted for. Rescuers on both sides of the border are searching for survivors while bracing for the possibility of a second flood, with the BBC reporting that fears of another surge have put rescue teams on edge.
Iran War Reaches Six Months With No Off-Ramp as Mediators Converge on Tehran
The US-Iran war reached its six-month mark on Friday with no end in sight, despite President Donald Trump's initial forecast that it would last four to five weeks, according to an AP review. A June memorandum of understanding that briefly paused hostilities has expired, and White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Thursday that 'no negotiations are happening right now.' The Strait of Hormuz, through which more than one-fifth of global oil and gas supplies once passed, has been largely closed since early March, with traffic down roughly 95 percent, Al Jazeera reports. Yet a flurry of high-level visits to Tehran suggests a renewed push for talks. Qatar's Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani is in Tehran on Thursday to discuss de-escalation and reviving failed negotiations, Al Jazeera reports, following visits by Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir and Oman's Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi. Iran and Oman have agreed on a temporary shipping route through the strait, and Qatar has stressed the need for the waterway to return to its pre-February 28 status. Washington, meanwhile, has pivoted from strikes to economic pressure, threatening to sanction countries that refuse to break trade ties with Iran, AP reports.
US Patriot Missile Stocks in Europe 'Beyond Critical' After Iran War Drawdown
The US military is experiencing a 'beyond critical' shortage of advanced missile interceptors in Europe, largely driven by the war with Iran, a US defense official in Europe and a NATO official told the Associated Press. The most concerning shortfall involves Patriot interceptors, which can shoot down Russia's high-speed ballistic missiles. US missile stocks in Europe have been moved to the Middle East, where US and Gulf allies have fired significant numbers of interceptors to thwart Iranian drones and missiles. The officials warned that in the event of a Russian ballistic missile assault on a NATO target, the alliance could be forced 'to take punch after punch in the mouth,' in the words of the US defense official, and would have 'very limited' capability to defend against even a single ballistic missile strike. Though a Russian attack on NATO is not imminently expected, the shortfall exposes a vulnerability in European air defense at a moment when the CIA director's secret trip to Moscow has opened a new channel between Washington and the Kremlin, the BBC notes.
Chad Accuses Sudan of Cross-Border Air Strike Killing 12, Widening the Sahel War
Chad has accused Sudan's army of launching an air strike on a fuel market near their shared border that killed at least 12 people and wounded seven, Al Jazeera reports, citing a Chadian security source who said the strike targeted a site where the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) refuel. The US embassy in Khartoum backed Chad's account, condemning the Sudanese army for the strikes on Thursday. Sudan's Foreign Ministry said it was surprised by the allegations and insisted its forces respect the sovereignty of its neighbours. The incident follows a Chadian claim last week that Sudan struck a military convoy more than 100km inside its territory in the eastern Ennedi region. Chad has raised its alert level to its highest point and deployed about 100 armoured vehicles and signal-jamming trucks near the border, a local source told Reuters. The strike comes against the backdrop of a Sudanese civil war between the army and the RSF that has lasted over three years and displaced millions, and which the UN warns threatens an entire generation.
Gaza Ceasefire at Risk of Collapse, Board of Peace Envoy Warns
A senior official on President Trump's Board of Peace has warned that a collapse of last October's Gaza ceasefire would be 'a point of no return' for the region, the BBC reports. Nickolay Mladenov, the Board's high representative for Gaza, told the UN Security Council that Israel's continuing air strikes and Hamas's incomplete disarmament both threaten the process. Israel has rejected the 15-point roadmap for Hamas's disarmament announced by the Board last month, insisting the group must fully disarm before any troop withdrawal, while Hamas has agreed to give up weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli pullout. At least 1,303 Palestinians, including 300 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures the UN considers reliable. Mladenov said the process had not stalled and that committees had been established to settle remaining questions, but warned that 'every use of force that does not answer an immediate threat' costs the process something hard to buy back. His account differs from that of Trump envoy Jared Kushner, who said after meeting Israel's prime minister that withdrawal would be discussed only once demilitarisation was 'done.'
Trump Renames Lake Ontario 'Lake America' as US-Canada Trade War Deepens
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Thursday renaming Lake Ontario 'Lake America' for the US geographic naming service, the Associated Press reports, in a symbolic escalation of his trade war with Canada. The order comes after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed late last week, the BBC notes. The renaming follows a series of escalating measures in the bilateral dispute, which has already seen Trump impose steep tariffs on Canadian goods and threats over energy exports. The move is largely symbolic — the lake is shared with Canada, which will not recognise the new name — but it signals the administration's willingness to escalate a dispute with its largest trading partner and closest ally. Canada has responded to earlier US tariffs with its own measures, and the collapse of talks has left the two economies in a state of heightened uncertainty over trade, energy and border issues.
The Bottom Line.
Today's dominant story is humanitarian: a Himalayan glacial collapse killed more than 390 people and left over 1,400 missing across the Nepal-China border, with citizens of more than 30 countries unaccounted for. Strategically, the US-Iran war passed its six-month mark with no off-ramp, even as Qatari, Omani and Pakistani mediators converged on Tehran and Washington's economic squeeze on Iran tightened — while the war's cost became visible in a 'beyond critical' Patriot missile shortage in Europe. The Sudan war is spilling into Chad, the Gaza ceasefire is fraying over disarmament sequencing, and the US-Canada trade war has escalated into symbolic territory. The common thread is a world in which multiple crises are compounding: a closed Hormuz, depleted Western munitions, and a cascade of regional conflicts that no single off-ramp yet resolves.

item.title: Strategic Brief — August 27, 2026: CIA Director's Secret Moscow Visit Opens a New Channel as Washington and Seoul Prepare Trilateral Drills
item.description:
CIA Director's Secret Moscow Visit Opens a New Channel as Washington and Seoul Prepare Trilateral Drills
A rare direct US-Russia intelligence channel surfaced this week even as the air war over Ukraine entered a deadlier phase, while Washington moved to rebuild trilateral military exercises with South Korea and Japan that Trump had earlier curtailed.
The CIA's Quiet Trip to Moscow
The New York Times reported that the CIA director made a secret visit to Moscow, and President Trump acknowledged the trip publicly, telling reporters that 'something may come of' it while describing the visit as 'semi-routine,' according to BBC and Sky News. The disclosure comes at a moment of acute tension: Bloomberg reports that Putin is moving to escalate the war in Ukraine with negotiations at a dead end, and the Wall Street Journal describes the Russia-Ukraine air war as having entered a new, deadlier phase. The CIA's outreach does not by itself signal imminent talks, but the fact that a direct US-Russia channel is being reopened at the intelligence level, and that the White House is choosing to acknowledge it, is a meaningful shift in atmospherics after months of near-total silence between Washington and Moscow.
The Air War Turns Deadlier
While diplomacy flickered, the fighting intensified. The Wall Street Journal reports the air campaign over Ukraine has entered a more lethal phase, and AP says Ukraine has extended its long-range drone campaign into Russia, destroying a Wildberries logistics depot. President Zelenskyy has warned, per CNN, that Russia is likely to mobilize at least 300,000 more troops, and Al Jazeera reports growing fears of a fresh Russian mobilization amid reports of intimidating recruitment tactics. Zelenskyy, meanwhile, visited the frontline and is pushing a reboot of Ukraine's defensive 'fortress belt' positions, according to The Guardian's war briefing. The picture is of a war grinding toward a larger Russian escalation even as both sides keep a diplomatic door ajar.
Washington Rebuilds Trilateral Drills With Seoul and Tokyo
The United States is preparing trilateral military exercises with South Korea and Japan, according to Türkiye Today, AzerNews and A News, a notable reversal given that President Trump had recently curtailed US-South Korea joint drills. North Korea appears to be responding to the renewed posture, firing a suspected missile toward the sea ahead of the planned exercises, per AP and NPR. Reuters, analyzing Trump's outreach to Kim Jong Un, warns the president's 'Kim gambit' is deepening allied doubts about US reliability at a key moment for Asia, even as the US redefines its South Korea relationship from a military alliance toward a broader economic partnership, per CNBC.
The Iran Pressure Campaign Widens
The US economic campaign against Tehran continued to expand. Treasury Secretary Bessent announced new sanctions aimed at blocking Iran's revenue streams, per PBS, and the New York Times reports Washington now intends to target more than oil — including gold, flights and cryptocurrency. Treasury has singled out Bank Melli, and Al Jazeera reports roughly 60 entities were targeted in the latest wave. Rubio has told allies the US is shifting from strikes toward sanctions as the primary instrument against Iran, according to Axios, a deliberate de-escalation of the military track. Iran, for its part, says the US is standing in the way of a Hormuz deal amid talks with Oman, per CNBC, and has vowed retaliation while emphasizing self-sufficiency, per NBC and Al Jazeera. AP reports there is so far no sign Tehran's leadership will bow to the pressure.
Gaza's Fragile Ceasefire Under Strain
In the Middle East, the Gaza ceasefire is fraying. The UN's deputy special coordinator for the peace process called the truce fragile, and Jerusalem Post reports the UN envoy Mladenov said Israel and Hamas are failing to uphold the ceasefire, harming the peace process. The US-led Gaza peace board has warned Hamas over kite attacks after an Israeli threat, per France 24, and the Washington Post reports the official leading Trump's Gaza ceasefire effort has publicly criticized Israel for its attacks. The International Crisis Group published analysis warning that resetting the ceasefire may rest on 'hollow promises,' while UN News notes children remain at risk in Gaza despite a drop in acute hunger.
The Bottom Line.
Today's most significant development is the reopening of a direct US-Russia channel via the CIA director's secret Moscow visit, even as the war in Ukraine edges toward a larger Russian escalation and a more lethal air campaign. Washington is simultaneously reasserting its Northeast Asia posture with revived trilateral drills with Seoul and Tokyo, while continuing to press Tehran economically and manage a Gaza ceasefire that is visibly fraying. The common thread is a US attempting to manage several simultaneous pressures — toward Moscow through backchannels, toward allies through renewed exercises, and toward adversaries through sanctions — without committing to a single decisive course.

item.title: Strategic Brief — August 26, 2026: US Removes Syria From Terror List, Ending Decades of Isolation as Washington Launches 'Economic Outcast' Campaign on Iran
item.description:
Washington formally delisted Syria from its state sponsors of terrorism list, clearing the last major barrier to the country's re-entry into the global financial system, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled a new wave of sanctions targeting Iran's trading partners.
Syria's Long Road Back to the Global Economy
The United States formally removed Syria from its state sponsors of terrorism list on Monday, completing a delisting process that began when President Donald Trump notified Congress on July 8 and passed a 45-day review period over the weekend, according to Al Jazeera. The designation had been in place since 1979, under Hafez al-Assad, and survived the regime's collapse in December 2024. Analysts told Al Jazeera the removal clears one of the last major hurdles to Syria's integration into the global financial system. Vittorio Maresca di Serracapriola, sanctions lead analyst for Karam Shaar Advisory, called it 'the last main barrier to banks reconnecting with the global community.' Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa said the country has 'shaken off' its past, and the delisting follows the earlier removal of sanctions on al-Sharaa and his Hayat Tahrir al-Sham movement. The economy remains weak, with nearly 90 percent of the population living below the poverty line, but the move is expected to ease financing and export restrictions that had deterred banks and investors.
Washington's 'Economic Outcast' Campaign Targets Iran's Trading Partners
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday announced a new round of sanctions on nearly 60 individuals and entities, describing the campaign as the 'economic asphyxiation' of Iran, according to Al Jazeera. 'Around the globe, our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,' Bessent said. The measures target networks accused of helping Iran generate oil revenue, procure weapons and conduct cyberoperations, spanning the Middle East, China, Singapore, Hong Kong and Europe. The push drew immediate pushback. China said it will safeguard its own interests, insisting sanctions will not resolve the conflict, while Qatar's Foreign Ministry called the measures unilateral, Al Jazeera reported. Iran's Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh rejected the sanctions, saying Tehran has programs to counter them. The campaign focuses on five sectors Washington says sustain Iran's economy: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping.
Pakistan's Army Chief Reports 'Significant Progress' in Tehran
Pakistan's Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi completed a daylong diplomatic mission to Tehran on Monday, and Pakistani officials said 'significant progress' was made in talks aimed at ending the US-Israel war on Iran, according to Al Jazeera. It was Munir's third visit to Iran this year. He met President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei. The Pakistani military said discussions focused on preventing further escalation, reopening the Strait of Hormuz and expediting the conflict's end, and on restoring the Islamabad MoU, the interim ceasefire framework that expired last week. Naqvi said the meeting 'concluded on a highly positive note.' Iran's Tasnim news agency quoted Pezeshkian as telling Munir the US 'must correct its tone and approach' and that American 'intimidation' would complicate implementing the MoU. The diplomatic push comes as Washington warns of severe penalties for any country supporting Iran and Tehran threatens to shut down Gulf oil exports.
UK Shares Missile Blueprints With Ukraine as Russia Warns of Attacks on British Factories
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham made Kyiv his first foreign trip on Monday, where Britain agreed to declassify blueprints for British-made components of the Scalp missile, a French-produced version of the Storm Shadow with a range of about 240km, according to Al Jazeera. The move lets Ukraine manufacture the long-range missiles domestically. Moscow reacted sharply. Kremlin adviser Andrei Fedorov told the BBC he could not 'exclude 100 percent' that there might be 'semi-military' action against Britain, suggesting drone factories producing for Ukraine could come under attack from 'unknown sources.' Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the UK is 'participating in this war' and adding 'fuel to the fire.' Burnham responded in Kyiv by asking reporters who started the fire in the first place. The escalation comes as Russia prepares for a winter offensive and reports grow of coercive recruitment tactics inside Russia, with Al Jazeera documenting alleged press-ganging in Penza and other cities.
Colombia's New President Vows Mass Deportations of Venezuelan Migrants
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, sworn in three weeks ago and closely aligned with Donald Trump, has promised to deport thousands of migrants without residence permits, mainly Venezuelans, as part of a crime-reduction push, according to the Associated Press. He said he would order the national immigration service to conduct raids with police as early as this week, targeting first migrants 'committing crimes' and then those living without regular status. 'I will not accept any illegal immigrants, wherever they come from,' de la Espriella said in a video. Around 2.8 million Venezuelans were living in Colombia as of August, according to the United Nations, the largest Venezuelan diaspora, with about 2.3 million holding temporary residence permits granted under a 2021 scheme. The policy marks a major shift for Colombia, which had long worked to protect and regularize incoming Venezuelans.
The day's defining development was Washington's formal removal of Syria from its terror list, a landmark that ends decades of isolation and opens the door to reconstruction financing, even as the US simultaneously escalated its economic war on Iran by sanctioning Tehran's trading partners under 'Operation Economic Outcast.' Pakistan reported significant progress in mediating the Iran conflict, the UK deepened its direct role in Ukraine by sharing missile blueprints, and Colombia's new president moved to deport Venezuelan migrants. The through-line is a Washington that is simultaneously reintegrating one former adversary, isolating another, and pushing allies and intermediaries to take sides in two overlapping wars.

item.title: Strategic Brief — August 25, 2026: US Pushes Nationwide Arms Embargo on Sudan as Washington Prepares Largest Visa Revocation in History
item.description:
Washington escalates on two fronts: a UN Security Council push to expand Sudan's arms embargo nationwide, and a plan to revoke up to 200,000 visas from asylum-seekers. Meanwhile the US-Canada trade war deepens and new Iran sanctions target third countries.
The United States is pressing the UN Security Council to expand Sudan's arms embargo from Darfur to the entire country, in a bid to choke off the external support that has sustained a war now in its fourth year. Trump's senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, Massad Boulos, told the Security Council on Monday that financial, military and political backing for both the government forces and the rival Rapid Support Forces remains a driver of the conflict, which has killed at least 59,000 people and displaced some 13 million, according to AP. The proposed US resolution would apply the embargo to all parties operating in Sudan's territory and explicitly reaffirm that drones and related technologies fall under it. Boulos did not name the countries providing support, but AP notes Egypt has backed the military while UN experts and human rights groups have accused the UAE of arming the RSF, a charge Abu Dhabi denies.
The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum in the United States, according to State Department documents obtained by AP and two US officials. The move, coordinated with the Department of Homeland Security, would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history and would likely face legal challenges. State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott confirmed the coordination, saying the department is identifying and revoking the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who came as short-term visitors but then filed for asylum. He declined to give a number, calling the process ongoing and rolling. Officials said most of those with pending asylum cases would be recategorized but would lose their business or tourism status, though the revocations would not necessarily mean immediate deportation.
The United States imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian products early Saturday, and Canada said it would retaliate beginning September 8 after last-ditch negotiations failed to resolve the latest strain between the historic allies, AP reports. Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Canada's response on Parliament Hill, while President Donald Trump told Canadian leaders to 'fall in line.' The escalation follows the collapse of talks that had been meant to head off a new round of tariffs. The dispute now carries real economic weight on both sides of the border, hitting steel and other industrial goods at a moment when supply chains are already under strain.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced new sanctions on Monday aimed at blocking all potential sources of revenue for Iran, including secondary sanctions on countries that continue to do business with Tehran, according to AP. The Iranian rial dropped to 2.02 million to the dollar as trading opened, extending a slide that began well before the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February. Iran warned of a harsh response to the new measures. In a sign of Tehran's diplomatic maneuvering, Iran's Parliament Speaker and top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf met Pakistan's Army Chief Field Marshal Gen. Asim Munir in Tehran on Monday. The secondary sanctions are the sharpest escalation yet of Washington's economic campaign, threatening to force third countries to choose between the US financial system and trade with Iran.
Israeli police arrested a 16-year-old boy from the Israeli settlement of Avigayil in connection with the beating of a 61-year-old Palestinian man with a pipe in the occupied West Bank, AP reports. The arrest comes amid a broader pattern of settler violence that has drawn international criticism and added friction to US-Israel relations. The incident is a reminder that the West Bank remains a live flashpoint even as attention focuses on Gaza and the wider Iran confrontation, with settler attacks and Palestinian casualties continuing to feed instability in the territory.
Today's developments show Washington escalating on multiple fronts at once: a UN push to expand Sudan's arms embargo nationwide, the largest mass visa revocation in US history, a deepening tariff war with Canada, and new secondary sanctions on Iran that force third countries to pick a side. The common thread is an administration willing to use economic and legal leverage aggressively against adversaries and allies alike. The Iran sanctions and the Sudan embargo both aim to cut external support to hostile actors, while the visa and tariff moves signal a harder line on immigration and trade. The risk is that these parallel confrontations compound each other, stretching US attention and diplomatic capital across the Middle East, Africa, and North America simultaneously.

item.title: Strategic Brief — August 24, 2026: US Readies 'Most Crushing Economic Operation' Against Iran as Tehran Calls Sanctions Support an 'Act of War'
item.description:
Washington is shifting the Iran conflict from the battlefield to a coordinated economic-isolation campaign aimed at collapsing the regime, with details due today. Canada walked away from trade talks with the White House, and a new peace roadmap emerged for eastern DR Congo.
The defining shift today is Washington's decision to wage economic war on Iran — a coordinated isolation campaign aimed at collapsing the regime, with details due at a press conference on 24 August and Tehran warning that supporting it would be an 'act of war.' That escalation, alongside Canada's decision to walk away from trade talks with the US, points to a world where economic coercion has become the primary instrument of great-power pressure. Meanwhile, a credible peace roadmap emerged for eastern DR Congo, Ukraine's political crisis deepened over wartime elections, and Thailand's southern insurgency flared in a coordinated arson wave. The common thread: the tools of statecraft are shifting from the battlefield to the balance sheet, and every ally is being forced to pick a side.

item.title: Strategic Brief — August 23, 2026: US-Canada Trade War Escalates as Talks Collapse, Washington and Ankara Friction Grows Over Israeli Strikes in Syria
item.description:
Washington imposed 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian goods after negotiations collapsed, deepening a rupture in the Western alliance. Separately, a US envoy says Israel struck Syria without notice and may have been baiting Turkey, exposing strain inside the anti-Iran coalition.
The defining development of the day is the collapse of US-Canada talks into a 50 percent tariff war, marking the clearest economic rupture yet inside the Western alliance, while the US-led camp against Iran shows internal strain as Washington's envoy accuses Israel of provoking Turkey with strikes in Syria. Iran is widening its own threat to alternative oil routes in response to fresh US pressure, and the Russia-Ukraine drone war continues to escalate on both sides of the border. The broadest picture is one of simultaneous fragmentation, as economic, military and climate pressures erode alliances and supply chains once taken for granted.

item.title: Strategic Brief — August 22, 2026: Iran Threatens NATO's Southeast Flank as War Nears Europe, US-Pakistan Spat Erupts Over Kashmir Visit
item.description:
Tehran warns it will strike Bulgaria's Bezmer Air Base and other European targets aiding US operations, while Washington pivots from military to economic pressure on Iran. Separately, a Trump envoy's Kashmir visit strains US-Pakistan ties.
The Iran-US war is entering a new phase: Tehran is threatening NATO's European flank even as both sides signal openness to ending the conflict, with Washington pivoting to a sanctions campaign and Iran insisting it negotiates from strength. The US re-designation of Hezbollah as an Iranian proxy widens the legal and financial front, while a Trump envoy's Kashmir remarks strain US-Pakistan ties and Bangladesh holds its first contested presidential vote in decades. The central question is whether the war can be contained to the Middle East or whether Europe's southeast becomes the next front.

item.title: Strategic Brief — August 21, 2026: Iran Weighs Strikes on US Bases in Europe as War Threatens to Leap the Mediterranean, Israel Bombs Syrian Base to Block Turkish Deployment
item.description:
Iranian sources tell the FT the IRGC has assessed US bases across Europe — including in Bulgaria — as contingency targets if the conflict widens, a move that would drag NATO territory directly into a war so far confined to the Gulf. Separately, Israel struck the Abu al-Duhur airbase in Syria to prevent a Turkish deployment, opening a new Israel-Turkey flashpoint, while Russia killed at least 13 people in a nine-hour barrage on Kyiv.
The defining shift of the day is geographic: Iran's reported contingency planning against US bases in Europe would, if realized, turn a Gulf war into a direct challenge to NATO territory and the logistics spine that feeds both that fight and Ukraine. That prospect lands alongside a new Israel-Turkey confrontation over Syria — Israel bombing the Abu al-Duhur base to block a Turkish deployment and drawing an unusual public rebuke from Washington — a brutal Russian strike on Kyiv, a Gulf conflict now fought largely through sanctions and trade cutoffs, and mounting strain in the West Bank and Sudan. The wars that began in the Middle East and Eastern Europe are showing clear signs of merging — with Turkey's expanding Syria role and Europe's hollowed-out air defenses as the vulnerable hinges.
